Four Hundred Silent Years
for HUN-dred SY-lent yeerz
noun phrase (the intertestamental period)
A traditional name for the intertestamental period between the prophecy of Malachi and the coming of John the Baptist, when no canonical prophet spoke in Israel.

Biblical Definition

The four hundred silent years are the intertestamental period—roughly four centuries between the last canonical prophet, Malachi, and the appearance of John the Baptist—during which no inspired prophet spoke the word of the LORD in Israel. They are “silent” not because nothing happened (these were the eventful years of Persian, Greek, and Roman dominion, of the Maccabees, the rise of the synagogue, and the parties of Pharisees and Sadducees) but because the voice of canonical prophecy was stilled, as Amos had foretold a famine, not of bread, but of hearing the words of the LORD. Malachi himself had sealed the Old Testament with a promise that bridged the silence: “Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me”; and “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD.” When at last the silence broke, it broke with the cry of John the Baptist in the wilderness, the promised messenger preparing the way, and then with the Word made flesh. The dictionary holds the silent years as a witness to the providence of God ordering history toward the fulness of time: through them He prepared the world—the synagogue, the Greek tongue, the dispersion, the Roman roads—for the swift spread of the gospel. It marks the period against two errors: the elevation of the apocryphal and intertestamental writings of these years to the level of canonical Scripture, which the dictionary rejects as the Protestant canon does; and the despairing notion that God had abandoned His people, when in truth He was silently arranging the stage for the greatest act of redemptive history, the coming of His Son.

Webster 1828 Definition

The intertestamental period of about four centuries between Malachi and John the Baptist, when no canonical prophet spoke (Amos 8:11); broken at last by the promised messenger (Malachi 3:1), the silence in which God prepared the world for the fulness of time.

FOUR HUNDRED SILENT YEARS, noun phrase. The intertestamental period between Malachi and John the Baptist.

“Silent” in that no canonical prophet spoke the word of the LORD (Amos 8:11).

Eventful in history: Persian, Greek, and Roman rule, the Maccabees, the synagogue.

Malachi's closing promise bridged the silence: “I will send my messenger” (Malachi 3:1).

Broken by John the Baptist and the coming of the Word made flesh.

Key Scripture

Am 8:11 — "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:"

Mal 3:1 — "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts."

Mal 4:5 — "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD:"

Mr 1:2 — "As it is written in the prophets, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee."

Modern Corruption

One error elevates the apocryphal writings of these years to canonical Scripture; the other reads the silence as God's abandonment, when in truth He was preparing the world for the fulness of time.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One live error concerns the canon. During the silent years arose the apocryphal and intertestamental writings—Maccabees, Tobit, Judith, Sirach, and the rest—which Rome received into its canon at Trent. The dictionary holds the Protestant canon: these books, however useful for history, are not inspired Scripture, and their very period is marked by the absence of the prophetic voice. The silence of those years is itself a witness that the Old Testament canon was closed with Malachi until the new prophetic dawn in John and in Christ.

The opposite error reads the silence as the abandonment of God, as though He had forgotten His people through four long centuries. The dictionary answers that the silence was not absence but preparation. Through those years the providence of God ordered the world for the gospel: the synagogue taught the Scriptures, the Greek tongue gave a common speech, the dispersion scattered worshippers of the true God among the nations, and Rome built the roads the apostles would walk. The silence ended exactly as Malachi promised, with the messenger preparing the way; and the four hundred years of waiting proved to be the ripening of the fulness of time for the coming of the Son.

Hebrew Roots

From the “silence” of canonical prophecy between Malachi and John; the “intertestamental” period named for its place between the two Testaments.

expand to see more

“Silent”: no canonical prophet spoke the word of the LORD in these centuries.

“Intertestamental”: the period between the Old and New Testaments.

Amos' “famine… of hearing the words of the LORD” foretells the silence (Amos 8:11).

Malachi's promise of the messenger bridges the silence (Malachi 3:1).

Broken by John the Baptist, the promised forerunner.

Usage

"The teacher described the four hundred silent years as God's preparation of the world for the fulness of time."

"He held the apocryphal writings of the period to be useful but not inspired Scripture."

"She saw that the silence was not abandonment but the ripening of the appointed hour."
